questiontext.text: Which operations does a deque (double-ended queue) support in O(1)?

answer.text: Insert and remove at both the front and the rear

feedback.text: Correct — a deque allows O(1) insertion and deletion at both ends.

answer.text: Insert only at the rear and remove only at the front

feedback.text: That describes a plain FIFO queue, not a deque.

answer.text: Insert and remove only at the front

feedback.text: A deque works at both ends, not just the front.

answer.text: Random access to the middle element in O(1)

feedback.text: A deque operates at its ends; arbitrary indexed access is not its defining O(1) operation.

generalfeedback.text: A deque supports O(1) insertion and removal at both the front and the rear.

questiontext.text: A deque can emulate which classic structures?

answer.text: Both a stack and a queue

feedback.text: Correct — using one end gives a stack; using opposite ends gives a queue.
It can also behave as a stack by using a single end.
It can also behave as a queue by enqueuing at one end and dequeuing at the other.

answer.text: Neither a stack nor a queue

feedback.text: A deque generalizes both.

generalfeedback.text: Because it operates at both ends, a deque can behave as a stack (LIFO) or a queue (FIFO).

questiontext.text: Which implementation gives a deque O(1) access at both ends?

answer.text: A circular array or a doubly linked list

feedback.text: Correct — both give O(1) work at the front and the rear.

answer.text: A singly linked list with no tail pointer

feedback.text: Without a tail pointer, rear operations are not O(1).
A heap orders by priority, not by both ends.
Hashing gives key lookup, not ordered end operations.

generalfeedback.text: A circular array or a doubly linked list supports O(1) insertion and removal at both ends.

questiontext.text: If you only ever push and pop at a single end of a deque, it behaves as a:

feedback.text: Correct — pushing and popping at one end is exactly a stack.
A deque does not order elements by priority.
A deque does not keep elements in sorted order.
A deque is a sequence, not a set.

generalfeedback.text: Using a single end for both push and pop makes a deque behave as a LIFO stack.

questiontext.text: A deque can be implemented with a circular array or a doubly linked list.

feedback.text: Correct — both a circular array and a doubly linked list give O(1) access to both ends.
Both a circular array and a doubly linked list are standard deque implementations.

questiontext.text: A deque only allows insertion and removal at a single end.

feedback.text: A deque works at both ends, not just one.
Correct — a deque supports operations at both the front and the rear.

questiontext.text: A double-ended queue allows insertion and deletion at ______ ends.

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.
Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about a deque are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It supports O(1) insertion and removal at both ends

feedback.text: Yes — that is its defining property.

answer.text: It can be implemented with a doubly linked list

feedback.text: Yes — a doubly linked list gives O(1) access to both ends.

answer.text: It provides O(1) indexed access to arbitrary positions

feedback.text: No — a deque operates at its ends, not at arbitrary indices.
No — it generalizes both LIFO and FIFO access.

generalfeedback.text: A deque: O(1) at both ends, implementable by circular array or doubly linked list, and can act as stack or queue.
